newsitem.title: USA: Harcourt deal to move publisher into new age.
newsitem.headline: Harcourt deal to move publisher into new age.

text.p: Harcourt General's proposed acquisition of National Education Corp will propel the traditional textbook publisher into a new age of education where teachers and students are miles apart.
Although analysts expect the $800 million deal to dilute short-term earnings, they said the benefits are tremendous.

"It takes Harcourt from being an old, established company looking to maintain the status quo to a company that is participating in the evolution of education," said Michael Moe of Montgomery Securities.

Harcourt earlier announced it had wrested National Education from a March merger with Sylvan Learning System Inc. Harcourt launched its rival and higher takeover bid for National Education in April and earlier this month announced the two companies had started friendly negotiations.
Originally worth $750 million, the value of the planned stock transaction between National Education and Sylvan eroded due to a decline in Sylvan's stock price.
Harcourt first offered $19.50 per share for National Education, but then raised the bid to $21 per share as the two companies entered friendly talks.

Based in Irvine, Calif, National Education provides education and training through correspondence schools and supplemental educational materials. It also owns 83 percent of Steck Vaughn Publishing Corp.

The deal comes as traditional education methods are increasingly supplemented with technology that allows students to access classes through computers and other equipment. Harcourt said National Education's products, services and distribution channels fits well with its publishing business.
"Now, Harcourt has a new launching platform for its products. It's ideal,' said Ivan Obolensky of Shields & Co.
Meanwhile, the collapse of the National Education-Sylvan deal won the approval of Sylvan shareholders, who bid the company's stock up 1-7/16 to 34-5/16 in early afternoon trade.
Analysts said shareholders had been concerned Sylvan's planned acquisition of National Education would slow the company's growth rate.
"I think this is a relief to a lot of the Sylvan shareholders," said Gerald Odening of Smith Barney.
The transaction calls for Harcourt to pay Sylvan a $30 million fee for breaking up its pact with National Education.

Analysts said Sylvan is likely to use that money for transactions that will build on its core tutoring and trade school business. The company last month announced plans to buy a privately-held company that provides remedial education.
"Sylvam has a very big appetite to create a large education company and it is a fertile field for growth. Sylvan is going to be right in the midst of it," Moe said.
Shares of Harcourt fell 1/2 to 46-4/8. National Education stock rose 3/8 to 20-7/8.
